rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: B caches the GET /api/tags result for 60s and invalidates it only when articles create tags. A makes article deletion remove orphan tags from the db, but nothing invalidates B's cache on that path. After merge, deleting an article that removes tag "solo" leaves the cache still serving "solo" for up to 60s (until TTL expiry or another article creation), even though the tag no longer exists. B's invariant ('refresh when tags change') is broken by A's new tag-removing path.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: B's userChangePassword hashes the new password with hashPassword and then passes it to userUpdatePrisma. After A's change, userUpdatePrisma hashes any provided password again. The result is a double-hashed password: bcrypt(bcrypt(newPassword)). Subsequent logins compare the plain new password against the double hash and fail, so a user who changes their password via POST /api/user/password gets locked out. B's tests do not catch this because they only check the stored password differs from plain text and from the old hash, never that login works afterward.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes Prisma auto-set Article.updatedAt on every update via @updatedAt (and removes the manual timestamp). Change B adds a views counter that is incremented via prisma.article.update on every GET of an article. Combined, every read now bumps updatedAt, since @updatedAt applies to any update call on the model, including the views increment. Previously, with the manual timestamp, only articleUpdatePrisma changed updatedAt. So an article's updatedAt (exposed in the article view) now changes on every read, no longer reflecting the last edit. Neither change alone has this behavior.

rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem: making sure the tag list does not show tags that no article uses anymore. Merged, the code does the job twice: once in the delete path and once in the read path, and the two even ship nearly identical integration tests asserting the same behavior. Either one alone makes the test pass, so one of the two mechanisms is redundant and should be removed. There is also a minor side difference (A would also clean up tags that were orphaned for other reasons, such as article updates, only at delete time, while B handles all cases), but the intent overlap is clear.

rows.explanation: Change A makes article updates rename the slug when the title changes. After the merge, once an article is renamed, every RecentView row for the old slug is orphaned. recentArticlesPrisma then looks up articles by those stale slugs, finds nothing, and silently drops them via flatMap. A user who viewed an article and then saw it renamed loses it from their recent list. The renamed article does not reappear under its new slug until it is viewed again. B's slug-as-key design assumes slugs are immutable, which was true before A, since the old code never changed them. Neither change is wrong alone, but together they produce a concrete wrong behavior.

rows.label: conflict

The cursor's key and the sort key disagree. If an article is edited, its updatedAt diverges from createdAt, so paging with ?after=<slug> can skip articles or repeat them. For example, with articles created in order 1,2,3 (list order 3,2,1) and article 1 edited last, after=2 yields articles with updatedAt < updatedAt(2), which now excludes article 1 (the one that should come next). Also, B's test sets updatedAt only and relies on updatedAt ordering; with A's createdAt ordering, creation order happens to match in the test so it passes, but the combined behavior is wrong in practice.

Concrete scenario: PUT /api/user/image with {image: "http://evil.example/a.png"} returns 200 and stores it, while PUT /api/user with the same image returns 400. A's agent task ('Require https images on user update') is undermined by B's route, an invariant violation neither change creates alone.

Conversely, typing the trimmed form works for confirm but the user may only remember the padded one. The new confirm endpoint thus applies a different password-comparison rule from the one A made canonical, so it wrongly rejects some correct passwords. B's tests don't hit this because they use passwords without whitespace.

rows.explanation: Change A soft-deletes articles by setting deletedAt and updates the article get, list, and feed queries to filter out deleted rows. Change B adds a tag counts endpoint that counts articles per tag using `_count: { select: { article: true } }` on the tag relation, which does not filter on deletedAt. In the merged code, a soft-deleted article keeps its row and its tag associations, so the counts endpoint still counts it. For example, after the only article tagged 'x' is deleted, GET /api/tags/counts still returns x with count 1, even though no visible article carries that tag. The `.filter(entry.count > 0)` was meant to hide unused tags but is defeated because soft-deleted rows still count. Previously, hard delete removed the join rows and the count was correct. The two changes are individually correct but together produce a wrong count.

rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem, email case/whitespace normalization on register and login, at different layers. Change A normalizes in the controllers via a new normalizeEmail helper, while Change B normalizes inside the DB helpers (userCreatePrisma and userGetEmailPrisma) with inline trim().toLowerCase(). Merged, every email is normalized twice: the controller normalizes, then the DB helper repeats the same logic. The behavior is correct and idempotent, but the work is duplicated and the logic lives in two places (the helper and inline copies), so one of the two should be removed. Each side also adds its own near-identical integration test.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes article slugs change on title update. Change B introduces a RecentView table keyed by (username, slug) with no foreign key to Article, so slug is stored as a plain string. Once a title rename changes an article's slug, existing RecentView rows keep the old slug. recentArticlesPrisma then looks up articles by the stale slug, finds none, and silently drops those entries via flatMap, so a user's recently viewed list loses an article after it is renamed. Before A, slugs were effectively immutable, so this dangling-reference assumption held. If a new article later reuses the old slug, the recent list would show the wrong article for that user. Neither change alone has this problem.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: After merging, articlesListPrisma orders by createdAt desc (A) but the new ?after= cursor filters with updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt (B). The cursor's sort key no longer matches the list's ordering key. Concretely: article X is created early but edited recently (updatedAt late), and article Y is created later but never edited. The list order is Y, X (by createdAt). Requesting ?after=Y filters updatedAt < Y.updatedAt, which drops X because X.updatedAt is later, so X is skipped. Conversely, articles that appear before the cursor in createdAt order but have an older updatedAt are returned again, giving duplicates. B's own test passes only because createdAt and updatedAt order are the same there. So pagination via the cursor breaks only when both changes are combined.

In the merged code, a user can set image to "http://..." via the new endpoint, which defeats the invariant A introduces (images must be https). This is a concrete scenario where the merged behavior contradicts A's intent: the rule is enforceable only on one of two paths that set the same field.

rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim passwords, so stored hashes are of trimmed passwords and login/register compare trimmed values. Change B adds userConfirmPassword, which deliberately bypasses compareWithHash and calls bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password) directly with the raw, untrimmed password. Merged, a user who registered with a password containing surrounding whitespace (e.g. "  secret ") has a hash of "secret"; login succeeds with either form, but confirm-password with the original "  secret " returns 403, and a user can confirm with "secret" but not with what they typed at registration. Conversely, a password with trailing whitespace entered at login (trimmed, accepted) is rejected by confirm-password. This inconsistency arises only from the combination: B's bypass breaks the invariant A introduces that all password comparisons trim.

Existing users whose passwords were hashed with leading/trailing whitespace (before the change) would fail both login and confirm-password equally, so there's no new inconsistency between the endpoints. B's integration test uses registerUser with a password presumably without whitespace, so it still passes. Logging additions in A don't interact with B's new controller. No concrete runtime or intent conflict.

rows.explanation: Change A makes hashPassword and compareWithHash trim passwords before hashing and comparing. Change B adds a confirm-password controller that calls bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password) directly, deliberately bypassing compareWithHash (to avoid its logging). Merged, any user who registers with a password that has leading or trailing whitespace gets a hash of the trimmed value (via A's hashPassword in register). Login (via compareWithHash) trims the input and succeeds. But confirm-password compares the untrimmed input against the hash, so the user who enters their real password (with whitespace) gets 403, and a user who enters the trimmed form also works only if they omit the whitespace, which is inconsistent with login. Conversely, a user who registers with 'secret ' and later enters ' secret' at login succeeds but confirm-password fails with the same input. This is a concrete runtime inconsistency: B's direct bcrypt use bypasses the normalization A introduced into the shared helper.

But confirm-password with ' secret ' (the exact value they registered with) compares untrimmed against hash of 'secret' and returns 403; only 'secret' works. This is inconsistent with login behavior and breaks the new invariant A establishes that surrounding whitespace is ignored for all password checks. B's code comment only avoided compareWithHash because it logged passwords, a log A removes, so the workaround is now both unnecessary and harmful. But that affects login equally and is a deliberate side effect of A's change, not an interaction with B. B's controller does not use A's logging, which is only a style gap rather than a conflict. A's change makes the first element the newest, which is consistent with B's intent, and B's explicit reduce works regardless. The logging changes don't touch B's new handler.
